sections.h2: What is the first step in selling a house quickly in Fair Lawn?
sections.html:
The first step is the Certificate of Continued Occupancy, which the borough requires before the title of a one or two family home can transfer. Everything else about a fast Fair Lawn sale, from price to closing date, depends on how soon the Building Department inspects the house and signs off.

Fair Lawn is a Bergen County borough about 12 miles northwest of New York City, and the Census counted 34,927 people there in 2020. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 37,128, a gain of 6.3 percent over the 2020 base. The borough covers only 5.14 square miles of land, so density is around 6,800 people per square mile and houses sit close together.

sections.h2: What is Fair Lawn's history, and how does it show in the housing?
sections.html:
Fair Lawn was farmland before it was a suburb, and the oldest houses on Berdan Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue still reflect that. Dutch and Irish settlers divided the land into large farm lots in colonial times, and Victorian homes went up along Berdan Avenue beside five Berdan family farms. The borough takes its name from Fairlawn, the estate David Acker built in 1865, which later became the Fair Lawn Municipal Building.

Residents petitioned to leave Saddle River Township because they felt the schools were poor value for the taxes they paid, and Fair Lawn became its own borough in 1924. Suburban growth came in three pockets: Memorial Park around River Road and Fair Lawn Avenue, Columbus Heights at Lincoln Avenue and Wagaraw Road, and Warren Point east of the railroad and south of Broadway.

Radburn, founded in 1929 as a town for the motor age, is one of the first planned communities in the United States and lies inside the borough. Eight sites in Fair Lawn are on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Radburn station and the Naugle House on Dunkerhook Road. If your home is near one, ask the building office whether any review applies before you change the exterior.

sections.html:

sections.h2: What does Fair Lawn's Certificate of Continued Occupancy involve?
sections.html:
Fair Lawn requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title in a one or two family dwelling, and the borough's published fee is $175. The Building Department is in Room 112 of the municipal building, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and its number is (201) 794-5307. Fire Prevention handles the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

  • An application and the $175 fee go in first, then the department inspects the property and may photograph conditions.
  • A smoke certificate from Fire Prevention, or a written waiver, is part of the file.
  • A failed public sidewalk must be repaired or replaced before the certificate is issued.
  • A buyer who flips the house must apply again as the seller at the next sale.

If a buyer will do the repairs, the borough offers a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only, with no occupancy. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming the buyer understands that, and after closing the buyer reapplies for the full certificate, paying another $175. On an as-is sale, the buyer must acknowledge that anything the inspection finds becomes the buyer's responsibility to correct.

sections.h2: How does the grid address system affect a Fair Lawn listing?
sections.html:
Most Fair Lawn addresses use a hyphenated number, such as the library's 10-01 Fair Lawn Avenue, and buyers who search online sometimes get no match unless they leave the dash out. Nearly 10,000 Fair Lawn addresses use this system, which accounts for almost half of the hyphenated addresses in New Jersey.

The first number tells you the block distance from Broadway on north-south streets, or the numbered street on east-west ones. Addresses south of Broadway or Route 4 begin with a zero. The system dates to at least the 1930s and was designed so emergency crews could find a house fast. Exceptions exist on the Glen Rock, Hawthorne and Saddle Brook sides and inside Radburn.

When you advertise the house, write the address both with and without the dash, and confirm it on the tax record so title and survey work match what appears on the deed.

sections.h2: Which roads, trains and neighborhoods define Fair Lawn?
sections.html:
Fair Lawn works as a commuter town because of two stations and two highways. Route 4 reaches the George Washington Bridge in under 10 miles from the Broadway district, and Route 208 runs northwest to Interstate 287. The Radburn and Broadway stations on NJ Transit's Bergen County Line serve Hoboken, with connections at Secaucus Junction to New York Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 144, 145, 148, 160, 164 and 196 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Local roads form a rough three-by-three grid: Saddle River Road, Plaza Road and River Road run north to south, and Broadway, Morlot Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue run east to west. The borough had about 99.6 miles of roadway in 2010, 84 of them municipal.

  • Berdan Grove: single-family streets around Berdan Grove Park, with the borough's highest concentration of Asian American residents.
  • Broadway District: the main shopping strip and a train stop at Warren Point and Lyncrest.
  • Radburn: the planned community with its own station and pathways.
  • Parks: Memorial Park, Berdan Grove Park, Gregory Park and Cresthill Park.

sections.h2: Which schools serve Fair Lawn, and who employs its residents?
sections.html:
Fair Lawn Public Schools run from prekindergarten through twelfth grade, with nine schools and 5,529 students in 2022 to 2023. Elementary schools are Forrest, Lyncrest, Milnes, Radburn, Warren Point and Westmoreland for kindergarten through fourth grade, and Memorial and Thomas Jefferson middle schools cover grades 5 to 8. Fair Lawn High School had 1,624 students and has been recognized as a Blue Ribbon School.

Employers include Columbia Bank, headquartered in the borough, Kuiken Brothers building materials, Zerega's pasta, and U.S. Technologies. The large Nabisco and Mondelez bakery on Route 208 operated from 1958 and was announced for closure in 2021, with demolition beginning in January 2023. The Fair Lawn Promenade, a mixed-use complex, opened on April 1, 2014. The Broadway shopping district continues to supply local retail jobs.

sections.h2: What are the closing steps and costs in Fair Lawn?
sections.html:
The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the Bergen County Clerk records the deed, and for a sale over $350,000 the fee runs from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $4.80 on the band from $200,000 to $550,000 and $5.30 per $500 between $550,000 and $850,000. Over $1 million, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller, and your attorney will calculate it.

Sellers who are New Jersey residents, including estates and trusts, complete a GIT/REP-3 to record the deed. For an estate sale, the executors who sign the deed also sign the form, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so a rejection should be resolved with the clerk's office first, then with the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275.

Property tax appeals in Bergen County go to the Board of Taxation at 201-336-6300, and its page says the filing deadline for 2026 assessment appeals has passed. For rent control questions on a rented house, the borough's rent leveling office is at (201) 564-6152.

faqs.q: Does Fair Lawn require an inspection before I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. The borough requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title in a one or two family dwelling. The fee is $175, and applications are made in Room 112 of the municipal building. Fire Prevention supplies the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take a Fair Lawn house that fails the inspection?
faqs.a: Yes, with a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming that the buyer understands there is no occupancy, and a failed sidewalk must still be fixed. After closing, the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175.

faqs.q: Who signs the GIT/REP form when an estate sells a Fair Lawn house?
faqs.a: The estate completes the form, signed by the executors who sign the deed or by the administrator if there is no will. An executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms, one for the estate and one personally. Residents use the GIT/REP-3.

faqs.q: Why do Fair Lawn addresses have a dash?
faqs.a: The dash comes from the borough's grid numbering system, in use since at least the 1930s. The first number counts blocks from Broadway or follows the numbered street, and addresses south of Broadway start with a zero. Many online forms only accept the number without the dash.

faqs.q: Which county office records a Fair Lawn deed?
faqs.a: The Bergen County Clerk records deeds, and the Bergen County Board of Taxation handles assessment appeals. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the GIT/REP form go in with the deed. Ask your closing attorney or title company to confirm the filing method for your closing date.
